newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Taiwan envoy protests at S.African China move.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan envoy protests at S.African China move.

text.p: Taiwan's ambassador to South Africa said on Thursday he had lodged a very strong protest with President Nelson Mandela's government over the downgrading of ties with Taiwan to open diplomatic relations with Beijing.

"At the instructions of my government...I lodged the strongest protest over what we see as the unfortunate announcement made by the South African government yesterday (Wednesday)," Ambassador I Cheng Loh told a news conference.
He said he had been given only 28 hours notice over the move and was very surprised by the "unusual" diplomatic practice.

Loh said Mandela informed him on Tuesday of Pretoria's intention to change its policy, but..."I thought he had given us 13 months to talk to the South African government" before the decision to recognise the communist Peoples' Republic became final.
"It is really quite unusual diplomatic practice...I am as surprised as you are about the timeframe because it does not conform to international practice," he said.

The envoy said he was "indeed led to believe through many statements by President Mandela, most recently in September, that relations would continue through the term of his office", which lasts until April 1999.
"We were entirely caught by surprise," said Loh, a 45-year-old veteran of Taiwan's diplomatic service who speaks fluent English.

Asked about a comment by South Africa's former president F.W. de Klerk that senior communists in Mandela's ruling bloc had influenced the decision, Loh replied: "I must confess I tend to agree with Mr de Klerk."

Loh said it was too early to say what the impact would be on trade between the two countries. Investment was another matter, he said, and there were "dozens of (joint) projects" which would now have to be reviewed by Taiwan's legislature.
Asked if Taiwan feared a diplomatic chain reaction in which South Africa's decision could influence the other 29 countries of the world with which it has relations, Loh said:
"I see no immediate danger of other countries following the lead of South Africa."
Loh recalled that he was present on October 24, 1971, when Taiwan was voted out of the United Nations.
"The sky didn't fall down. Taiwan continued to prosper. It only prospered more," he said.
Loh said the Mandela government's decision was a temporary setback and not the loss of a battle. "We do not regard this as a crushing blow," he added.
But he said Taiwan still hoped ..."they'll see their way clear to reconsider their decision".

The Taiwanese envoy said he had received many phone calls and faxed messages of support from a broad spectrum of South Africans who strongly disagreed with the decision to ditch formal ties with his country.
China sees Taiwan as a renegade territory and has sought to push the island into diplomatic isolation but Taiwan insists its 21 million people should have a voice in international affairs.

South Africa has been the biggest of only 30 states to recognise Taiwan and has had full relations with Taipei for 20 years. It is South Africa's seventh-largest trading partner with trade totalling 5.7 billion rand ($1.25 billion) in 1995.
